newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FOCUS-Pakistan's rupee devaluation jolts markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pakistan's rupee devaluation jolts markets.

text.p: Pakistan's central bank on Tuesday slashed 3.79 percent off the rupee's dollar value, sending stocks and cotton prices tumbling.
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), abruptly breaking a pattern of gradual downward adjustments, cut the rupee rate to 36.9700/37.1549 to the dollar from 35.6200/35.7981 fixed on August 29.
In the kerb market, the rupee immediately plunged 1.20 rupees to 40.50 to the dollar from Monday's close of 39.30.
Gold rates rose 90 rupees to 5,024 from Monday's 4.934, but the Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index fell 19.87 points, or 1.47 percent, to 1,332.14 in panic selling.
Cotton rates fell as the devaluation will make exports more competitive, brokers said.
SBP governor Muhammad Yaqub said the devaluation would strengthen Pakistan's economy and would have a nominal effect on the cost of foreign debt servicing.
"This action is to strengthen and not to weaken the economy," he told a news conference after the devaluation, which the bank calculated at 3.65 percent but foreign bankers at 3.79.
The devaluation came as a surprise to commercial bankers who said it reflected continuing balance of payments difficulties.
"The devaluation is contrary to expectations, as most people were prepared for a gradual adjustment, not a one-step devaluation," analyst Zuna Mansoor at ING Barings said.
"We expect the rupee depreciation for the (calendar) year to touch nine or 10 percent, and a worsening of the current account deficit, given inelastic imports."

A foreign economist, who asked not to be named, said Yaqub had apparently tried to foil speculators by delaying any adjustment and then devaluing the currency to bring it back into line with the SBP's dollar-dominated basket.
The SBP move comes ahead of planned talks between Pakistan and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the sidelines of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Washington this month.
Pakistan is trying to persuade the IMF to resume disbursements of a $600 million standby loan which have been delayed by uncertainty about the 1996/97 budget (July-June).

The IMF, which has voiced concern about Pakistan's balance of payments position, wants Islamabad to explain how it will cut its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product this year. The target was set in the budget unveiled in June, but various interest groups have since won tax concessions.
Bankers said they expected the rupee, which has fallen 5.31 percent since July 1 and 7.95 percent since January 1, to erode another three percent against the dollar by the end of 1996.
He said the rupee's weakness was unlikely to boost exports substantially, but could encourage remittances from Pakistanis working abroad and help Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves.
An executive at a foreign bank in Karachi said the central bank move could also prompt foreign fund managers to slow liquidation of their equity holdings in Pakistan and deter capital flight.
Foreign reserves, including gold and Special Drawing Rights, fell to $2.344 billion in August from $2.463 billion in July and $2.821 billion in August last year.
Pakistan's trade deficit widened to $270 millin in July from $95 million in June while the gap for the whole of 1995/96 yawned to $3.07 billion from $2.257 billion in 1994/95.
